description: ASTROGUARD is an interactive space mission training and survival simulator designed to educate students about life on the Moon and Mars. Using NASA's open datasets, users manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, and energy while handling challenges like solar storms, dust storms, and equipment failures. An AI-powered mission assistant provides survival recommendations and guidance, making space exploration engaging, educational, and interactive.

# AstroQuest — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

AstroQuest is an interactive, browser-based platform designed to introduce students to the challenges of living and working on the Moon. It places users in the role of junior astronauts, allowing them to explore a virtual lunar settlement and understand the systems required to maintain a lunar outpost.

The application features four sections: Lunar Habitat, Lunar Explorer, Science Center, and Mission Journal. The Lunar Habitat showcases facilities such as crew quarters, life-support systems, greenhouses, laboratories, and power stations. The Lunar Explorer encourages lunar discovery, while the Science Center introduces scientific concepts related to space exploration. The Mission Journal provides learning activities and mission objectives.

AstroQuest makes space education engaging through visualization, exploration, and mission-based learning. Users explore habitat systems and understand the importance of oxygen, water, food, energy, safety, and teamwork.

The project uses React and Vite, GitHub for source-code management, and Vercel for public deployment. Its architecture supports future NASA resource integration and additional educational content.

AstroQuest aims to inspire curiosity, promote STEM education, develop problem-solving skills, and help the next generation understand human exploration beyond Earth.

# AstroQuest — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

AstroQuest: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based learning experience that introduces young learners and the public to the challenges of living and working on the Moon. Instead of presenting space exploration only through facts, photographs, or slides, AstroQuest places users in the role of a junior astronaut responsible for helping establish and maintain a lunar outpost. The project turns a Moon settlement into a guided mission where users explore, make decisions, and understand habitat systems, resources, safety, and teamwork.

## WHAT WE DEVELOPED

We developed AstroQuest as a web application with a space-inspired interface and an interactive lunar-outpost experience. Its areas include Lunar Habitat, Lunar Explorer, Science Center, and Mission Journal.

The main experience is a simulated lunar settlement. Users can examine an outpost and its important components, including crew quarters, life-support facilities, a greenhouse, a laboratory, a power station, and other infrastructure. These facilities show how a Moon base depends on systems working together.

We also developed the project around mission-based interaction and simulation. Users explore scenarios, consider choices, and learn through participation. A mission trainer is more engaging when the learner has a responsibility or objective rather than being only a reader. AstroQuest therefore frames activities around the work of an astronaut: exploring the environment, protecting the crew, maintaining the outpost, and discovering what is required to live away from Earth.

The project incorporates a NASA-data integration approach to connect learning with real space information. NASA resources can provide authentic context for lunar exploration, scientific discoveries, and mission planning. The application architecture separates the user interface and simulation experience from the data integration layer, making it easier to maintain the site and extend it with additional learning content or missions.

AstroQuest is built as a modern web project using a React-based interface and a Vite development and build workflow. This supports reusable components, responsive layouts, and efficient development. The source code is maintained in GitHub, and the application is deployed through Vercel. The public deployment makes it easy to share with students, educators, teammates, and judges.

## HOW IT ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge calls for an engaging way to help learners understand astronaut activities and the realities of space exploration. AstroQuest addresses this goal by changing the learning format from passive information consumption to interactive participation. A user is not merely told that astronauts need oxygen, energy, food, shelter, and scientific equipment; the user encounters those needs as part of an outpost and can connect each requirement to a visible facility or mission objective.

First, AstroQuest makes complex ideas easier to understand through visualization. A lunar habitat is an abstract concept for someone who has never studied space systems. Showing crew quarters, a greenhouse, a power station, and life-support infrastructure in one environment gives learners a mental model of how a settlement is organized. The scene prompts questions: Why does the habitat need power? What happens if life support fails? How can plants support a crew? Why is a laboratory important?

Second, the project uses a mission-oriented structure to encourage active learning. Exploration and mission activities invite users to set goals, observe the environment, and think about decisions. A trainer can make learning memorable by asking a learner to respond to a situation, not simply recall a definition. AstroQuest's simulation concept provides a foundation for such experiences, including future scenarios involving resource management, environmental hazards, equipment checks, and crew safety. This makes decision consequences understandable.

Third, AstroQuest connects a fictional training setting with authentic space knowledge. Integrating NASA information or linking learners to NASA material gives the project a credible scientific foundation and encourages users to explore beyond the application. The project is not intended to replace professional astronaut training; it is an introductory educational trainer that makes space exploration concepts approachable.

Fourth, the web format reduces barriers to access. A browser-based experience can be opened on a computer or compatible mobile device without a specialized installation. Public deployment lets people try and share the project easily.

## WHY IT IS IMPORTANT

Human exploration of the Moon represents a major step in scientific discovery and the development of capabilities for future missions. Understanding life on another world is both an engineering problem and an educational opportunity. Young learners need accessible ways to connect astronomy, physics, biology, engineering, computing, and environmental science with real missions. AstroQuest brings these disciplines together in a setting that can spark curiosity and help learners see how STEM knowledge is applied.

The project is important because it presents space exploration as a system of practical responsibilities. Astronauts must work in a dangerous and unfamiliar environment where resources are limited and equipment is essential. A lunar outpost needs reliable energy, protection from environmental conditions, breathable air, water, food, communication, and scientific tools. Introducing these needs through an interactive settlement can help learners appreciate the complexity of exploration and the importance of planning, maintenance, and cooperation.

AstroQuest can also support curiosity and confidence. Visuals and guided missions provide an entry point. Exploring first and asking deeper questions later can encourage independent learning and interest in STEM careers.

The project also demonstrates the educational potential of open and public space resources. NASA publishes information, imagery, and scientific material that can inspire learning. Using credible resources responsibly helps students distinguish evidence-based information from unsupported claims and gives them a path to further research. AstroQuest can serve as a bridge between a simple interactive experience and the broader body of knowledge produced by space agencies and researchers.

From a technology perspective, the project shows how web development can support science communication. A responsive interface, reusable components, simulation logic, and data integration can combine to create an experience that is more engaging than a static webpage. Public hosting enables access and improvements through testing and feedback.

## LEARNING EXPERIENCE AND FUTURE SCOPE

AstroQuest is designed around a simple learning journey: enter the lunar environment, explore the outpost, understand the purpose of its systems, and participate in mission activities. The Mission Journal can provide a place to review objectives or reflect on progress, while the Science Center can connect activities to explanations and scientific concepts. The Lunar Explorer area can encourage observation and discovery, and the Lunar Habitat can focus attention on the infrastructure required for survival. Together, these areas create a coherent experience rather than a collection of unrelated pages.

The project can be expanded with structured missions for different age groups and difficulty levels. Beginner missions could introduce the Moon, astronaut roles, and habitat components. Intermediate missions could ask users to balance energy, food, water, and equipment priorities. More advanced activities could introduce scientific experiments, navigation, communication delays, or emergency planning. Feedback, progress indicators, badges, and a mission journal could help learners understand what they have completed and what they have learned.

Further development could include more detailed simulation rules, additional NASA datasets, accessible audio or text guidance, multilingual content, and improved mobile controls. Classroom features could provide educator-led activities or group missions. Any future expansion should preserve scientific accuracy, explain assumptions, and avoid presenting simplified simulation results as real mission predictions.

## DESIGN PRINCIPLES

The design prioritizes clarity, discovery, and a sense of purpose. A space-themed interface establishes the setting, while readable labels and familiar navigation help users understand where to go next. The outpost is presented as a place with meaningful functions, so learners can associate each structure with a real need. This balance matters: visual effects should attract attention, but they should never obscure the educational message.

The project also treats learning as an iterative process. A learner can explore at their own pace, revisit an area, and connect information across different sections. The trainer can introduce concepts through context and reinforce them through missions. It gives educators a flexible starting point for discussions about habitats, sustainability, scientific experiments, and the engineering decisions behind human exploration for learners, educators, and curious future explorers.

## CONCLUSION

AstroQuest — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer — is a browser-based educational project that makes lunar exploration approachable through an interactive Moon-outpost environment. We developed a visual lunar habitat, mission-focused navigation, an exploration and learning structure, a simulation-oriented experience, and an architecture prepared for NASA information integration. By connecting visible habitat systems with astronaut responsibilities, the project helps users understand that living on the Moon requires science, engineering, planning, resource awareness, and teamwork.

AstroQuest addresses the challenge by encouraging learners to explore and participate instead of only reading about space. It is important because it can inspire curiosity, strengthen STEM learning, and make authentic space knowledge more accessible. Its public deployment and extensible web architecture provide a foundation for continued improvement. Ultimately, AstroQuest aims to help learners imagine themselves as responsible explorers, understand the challenges of a lunar mission, and become more interested in the science and technology that make future exploration possible.

It encourages learners to ask questions, test ideas, recognize interconnected systems, and appreciate the people and technologies that support safe exploration beyond our planet together.
